title: Trade-off communication
task_statement: Compare options on priced, measured trade-offs and tell each audience the facts it decides on. (Inference: wording from secondary sources)

components.name: Model pricing and cost per task
components.first_principle: Compare options on cost per completed task, because the completed task is the unit that you pay for.
steps: Read the token counts in the usage field of each response.
Price each token count at the rate for its token type.
Sum the prices across all requests for one completed task.
Compare the cost per completed task across the options.
Date the price table before each decision. (Inference)
pros: Shows the cost of a finished task, instead of a token rate alone.
Makes a cheap per-token option comparable with a costlier one.
Matches the usage fields that each response already returns.
cons: Prices change, so a comparison goes stale.
A cost per task needs task-level logs or evaluation results. (Inference)
use_when: Two models or platforms meet the quality bar at different prices.
A budget owner must approve a monthly spend.
do_not_use_when: Only one model meets the quality bar and no cost cap applies. (Inference)
The task volume is too small to change the budget. (Inference)

components.name: Cost per task measurement
components.first_principle: Record cost per task beside each quality score, so a trade-off shows both values together.
steps: Pull a sample of tasks from production logs, weighted like real traffic.
Write an outcome check for each sampled task.
Run each model tier across the effort levels.
Price each request from its usage fields.
Plot the score against the spend for each run.
Confirm the total with the Usage and Cost API.
Run the winner in shadow on a traffic slice before cutover.
pros: Shows whether a cheaper tier meets the quality bar on real tasks.
Shows a score and a spend for each option, so the trade-off stays visible.
Gives the same method for every model change. (Inference)
cons: Needs production logs and outcome checks that many teams lack. (Inference)
Results reflect the list prices at the time of measurement.
use_when: A model or effort change must pass a cost and quality review.
Two configurations score close to each other on quality.
do_not_use_when: The team has no production logs and no outcome checks yet. (Inference)
The budget has no limit, so the cost figure changes no decision. (Inference)

constraints.combination: Poll no more than once per minute for sustained use.

components.name: Five-field trade-off record
components.first_principle: Each option needs the same fields, so every audience reads the same facts. (Inference)
steps: List each option with the same set of fields. (Inference)
Fill the benefit field with a measured value and its evaluation set name. (Inference)
Fill the cost field with cost per completed task. (Inference)
Name the risk and the reversal cost of each option. (Inference)
Write one message for each audience that reads its own fields. (Inference)
Date every figure and set a review date. (Inference)
pros: Each audience decides on the facts it owns. (Inference)
Dated figures show when a choice needs review. (Inference)
cons: Several messages take more time than one summary. (Inference)
Figures drift when prices change, so the record needs a review date.
use_when: Several audiences hold budget, risk, or sign-off. (Inference)
The option has a material cost or a compliance impact. (Inference)
do_not_use_when: One person decides and holds all the facts. (Inference)
The choice is a small, fully reversible setting. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Name the signed approver for each audience. (Inference)
constraints.combination: Add a compliance impact field for regulated data. (Inference)

constraints.choice: State cost per completed task with the price date.
Report a percentile latency for each option. (Inference)
Estimate the reversal cost in days or weeks. (Inference)

components.exam_tie: D6.2. Expect an option that promises perfect accuracy or zero risk. The credited answer states the measured figure and its uncertainty. (Inference)
components.trap: One slide for all audiences looks efficient, but each audience then lacks the field it decides on. (Inference)
components.decision_rule: Give each audience the fields it decides on, and state the uncertainty beside each one. (Inference)
components.exam_tip: An option that claims perfect accuracy or zero risk has no measurement behind it.

decision_flow:
flowchart TD
  A{Audience holds budget or sign-off?} -->|Yes| B[Quantified option with priced fields]
  A -->|No| C{Several audiences decide?}
  C -->|Yes| B
  C -->|No| D[One message is enough]
  B --> E{Option claims perfect accuracy or zero risk?}
  E -->|Yes| F[Replace claim with measured figure and uncertainty]
  E -->|No| G[Send one message per audience]
cheatsheet:
flowchart LR
  P[Price per token] --> T[Cost per completed task]
  T --> S[Score beside cost]
  S --> F[Five fields]
  F --> A[One message per audience]
  F --> D[Date each figure]
  X[Perfect claim] --> M[Measured figure with uncertainty]

patterns.wording: a vendor claim of perfect accuracy or zero risk
patterns.rule: Replace each absolute claim with a measured figure and its uncertainty.
traps: Promise zero risk to win approval
Quote one accuracy figure without its evaluation set

patterns.wording: options that differ in price and quality for several audiences
patterns.rule: Price each option per completed task, then write one message per audience.

patterns.wording: a cheaper model proposed for a quality-sensitive task
patterns.rule: Measure quality and cost per task on real traffic before a switch.
traps: Switch on the lowest per-token price
Accept the cheaper tier without a test
